cases.prompt:
I'm using @lit-labs/router. I call `this._router.goto('/dashboard')`
inside a click handler, and the new route renders, but the URL
bar doesn't change and the browser back button is broken. What's
going on?

rubric.name: explains goto does not push history
mentions <a href> link interception
rubric.why: the cleaner alternative — the router intercepts these

skill.text: ## Why this happens `Router.goto()` is intentionally a "render only" operation — it matches the path against your routes and updates the rendered outlet, but it **does not push (or replace) anything on `window.history`**. So the URL bar is whatever it was before, and the browser's back/forward stack has no entry for the navigation, which is exactly why the back button does nothing useful. This trips a lot of people up because the name `goto` sounds like a full navigation, but it's really `setRoute` under the hood. ## Two ways to fix it ### 1. The cleanest fix: use a real link The `Router` (the top-level one you instantiate once per page) installs a global click listener that intercepts same-origin `` clicks, calls `history.pushState` for you, and then runs `goto()` internally. So this just works: ```html Dashboard ``` Back button, URL bar, deep-linking — all correct, no JS in your click handler at all. Prefer this whenever the click target is semantically a link. ### 2. If you really need an imperative call Push the history entry yourself, then call `goto`: ```ts private _onClick(e: Event) { e.preventDefault(); history.pushState({}, '', '/dashboard'); this._router.goto('/dashboard'); } ``` Use `history.replaceState` instead of `pushState` if you don't want the navigation to land in the back stack (e.g. a redirect after login). ## Quick gotcha to double-check Make sure you only have **one** `new Router(...)` on the page. If you've created additional `Router` instances for nested sections (instead of using the `Routes` controller), their global click/popstate listeners will fight each other and you can see symptoms that look a lot like "URL doesn't update."

rubric.name: explains goto does not push history
mentions <a href> link interception
rubric.why: the cleaner alternative — the router intercepts these

judge.reasoning: Both answers correctly explain that goto() does not push history and recommend both history.pushState and <a href> links. Answer B is more complete and idiomatic, adding the crucial popstate listener for back/forward button support, a clear rule of thumb for when to use each approach, and better explanation of why link interception handles edge cases like modifier-key clicks. Answer A has a useful but somewhat tangential note about multiple Router instances.

per_criterion.name: explains goto does not push history

cases.prompt:
I have a `@lit-labs/router` route with path `/users/*` for a
nested users section. When I navigate to `/users` (no trailing
slash), the route doesn't match. Why, and what do I do?

baseline.text: ## Why `/users` doesn't match `/users/*` `@lit-labs/router` builds its patterns on top of **URLPattern** semantics. In a pattern like `/users/*`, every character is significant — including the literal `/` between `users` and `*`. The `*` matches a wildcard segment, but the `/` *before* it is required. So when the URL is `/users` (no trailing slash), URLPattern sees: - Pattern: `/users/*` → expects `/users` + `/` + (anything, including empty) - URL: `/users` → missing the required `/` → no match. `/users/` and `/users/anything` both match; bare `/users` does not. ## What to do You have two clean fixes — pick whichever fits your app. ### 1. Always link with the trailing slash (simplest) Make sure every link, redirect, and `goto()` call uses `/users/`: ```html Users ``` ```ts this._routes.goto('/users/'); ``` This is the easiest fix and keeps your route table small. ### 2. Register both paths If you can't control every inbound link (e.g. external links, bookmarks, server-rendered URLs), register `/users` and `/users/*` as two routes pointing at the same render: ```ts this._routes = new Routes(this, [ { path: '/users', render: () => this._renderUsers() }, { path: '/users/*', render: () => this._renderUsers() }, ]); ``` Or normalize on entry by redirecting the bare form: ```ts { path: '/users', enter: async () => { this._routes.goto('/users/'); return false; } }, { path: '/users/*', render: () => this._renderUsers() }, ``` ### What *not* to do Don't try to make `*` match the missing slash by writing `/users*` — that pattern matches `/usersanything` (e.g. `/usersettings`), which is almost never what you want for a nested section. ### TL;DR URLPattern requires the literal `/` in `/users/*`, so `/users` is a non-match by design. Either always link to `/users/`, or register `/users` alongside `/users/*`.

rubric.name: recommends adding trailing slash to links
mentions registering both paths as alternative

skill.text: ## Why it doesn't match `@lit-labs/router` compiles each `path` string into a [`URLPattern`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/URLPattern), and **`URLPattern` matching is literal, character-for-character**. The pattern `/users/*` is parsed as: - the literal text `/users/` - followed by `*`, which is a wildcard group meaning "zero or more characters" The wildcard is **after** the second `/`, so the pattern requires that slash to be present in the URL. `/users` has no trailing slash, so it never even gets to the wildcard part — the literal prefix fails to match. (`*` matches zero characters, which is why `/users/` does match — the wildcard part is allowed to be empty, but the slash before it is not.) This is just standard URLPattern / path-to-regexp semantics; lit-labs/router isn't doing anything special here. ## What to do You have three reasonable fixes; pick based on intent. **1. Make sure links/navigation include the trailing slash.** This is the simplest fix if `/users/` is really the canonical URL of the section: ```html Users ``` Since the router intercepts same-origin clicks, this Just Works. **2. Register both paths.** If you want both `/users` and `/users/anything` to hit the same view, declare two routes: ```ts this._routes = new Routes(this, [ { path: '/users', render: () => html`` }, { path: '/users/*', render: () => html`` }, ]); ``` **3. Redirect `/users` → `/users/`.** If you want a single canonical URL, give `/users` an `enter` hook that rewrites: ```ts { path: '/users', enter: async () => { history.replaceState(null, '', '/users/'); return false; // don't render this route; let the next match handle it }, } ``` For most apps, option 1 (just write the slash in your links) is the cleanest, and option 2 is the most forgiving if users might type or bookmark the URL by hand.

rubric.name: recommends adding trailing slash to links
mentions registering both paths as alternative

judge.reasoning: Both answers are excellent and cover all three rubric criteria thoroughly. Answer A provides a slightly cleaner explanation of the URLPattern semantics with the bullet-point breakdown, and adds a useful 'what not to do' warning about `/users*`. Answer B provides a clearer explanation of why `/users/` does match (the wildcard can be empty, but the slash is required) and presents three options more cleanly. Both are essentially equivalent in quality and correctness.

per_criterion.name: recommends adding trailing slash to links
mentions registering both paths as alternative

cases.prompt:
What's the difference between `git merge` and `git rebase`?
Just a short, plain explanation.

baseline.text:
**git merge** combines two branches by creating a new "merge commit" that ties their histories together. Both branches' histories are preserved as-is, including the point where they diverged and rejoined.

**git rebase** moves your branch's commits on top of another branch, replaying them one by one. This rewrites history to make it look like your work happened linearly after the other branch, with no merge commit.

In short:
- **Merge** = preserves history, adds a merge commit (non-linear).
- **Rebase** = rewrites history, keeps it clean and linear.

Rule of thumb: merge for shared/public branches, rebase for cleaning up your local work before sharing.

skill.text:
**git merge** combines two branches by creating a new "merge commit" that ties their histories together. Both branches' histories are preserved as-is.

**git rebase** moves your branch's commits on top of another branch, rewriting them as if you'd started from there. The result is a clean, linear history with no merge commit.

Quick rule of thumb:
- Use **merge** to preserve history (good for shared branches).
- Use **rebase** to keep history tidy (good for your own local work before sharing).

judge.reasoning: Both answers are essentially equivalent in accuracy, clarity, and usefulness. They cover the same core concepts (merge commit vs. linear history rewrite) and offer the same practical rule of thumb. Answer B adds a small detail about 'replaying commits one by one' and 'non-linear' labeling, but neither is materially better than the other.
